info.bodyText: Skip to content Game Board The games The receipts About GitHub ↗ Three games. No hands. A person typed 8 prompts. An AI agent wrote the rest: three games, every system in them, the tests and the fixes. Play them, then read the receipts. Play the games Open the receipts → deepseek-v4.1-flash · 15 specialist agents Every figure below is summed from session logs — not an estimate. First Hearth — One wanderer, an unnamed valley, and a lit hearth. Everything else is history. Civilization simulation · 3 prompts · 9.0 h of agent work What it took 8 prompts typed by a human 3,103 agent steps, lead and subagents 23.6 h agent work (parallel agents summed) 922.9M tokens processed 3,469 tool calls 268 files written (a floor) Note Of those 922.9M tokens, 904.6M are cache reads — context the model re-used rather than wrote. Fresh output is 4.6M tokens. Agent-hours sum parallel subagents; wall-clock time is longer because the sessions sat idle overnight. The receipts page breaks all three clocks apart. The shelf three genres, three very different ways of getting there First Hearth — Civilization simulation · 136 files · 3 prompts First Hearth Civilization simulation / TypeScript · Vite · Canvas 2D · Vitest One wanderer, an unnamed valley, and a lit hearth. Everything else is history. 112x112 seeded worldgen with rivers, biomes, deposits and 3-5 AI neighbours Citizens with names, families, skills, morale and private thoughts 84 unit tests, 62 browser checks, 60 fps at 4x speed with 140+ population 3 prompts 9.0 h agent work 411.9M tokens 1,434 agent steps Play First Hearth ↗ How it was made → Mouse and keyboard; touch pans the map Blade & Mount — 3D melee tournament · 124 files · 4 prompts Blade & Mount 3D melee tournament / TypeScript · Vite · Three.js · WebGL2 Sixteen fighters, four rounds, and the whole yard watching. Four-directional attack and guard system with reach, speed and armour penetration Head, torso and leg hit zones; speed bonus from stepping into a strike 112 unit tests; runtime-generated arena, crowd, props and retargeted KayKit animations 4 prompts 14.0 h agent work 497.7M tokens 1,570 agent steps Play Blade & Mount ↗ How it was made → Keyboard and mouse required — no touch controls Alien Shooter — Top-down arena survival · 8 files · 1 prompt Alien Shooter Top-down arena survival / Vanilla JS · Canvas 2D · Web Audio · No build step You are the last survivor on colony XR-7. The nests have opened. Five enemy archetypes: crawlers, skitters, spitters, brutes and wave bosses 16 upgrades across stats and rare drops, plus XP magnet and dash i-frames Zero dependencies, zero build: plain HTML, CSS and Canvas 2D 1 prompts 39 m agent work 13.3M tokens 99 agent steps Play Alien Shooter ↗ How it was made → Mouse and keyboard, or touch The engine room The human never opened an editor. DeepSeek Harness is an agent runtime: it hands a model tools — a shell, a file system, a real browser, a shared task board — and the model works the way a small studio would. For the two larger games a lead agent split the work and spawned specialists: an arena artist, a character artist, a combat AI, a UI and audio engineer, a QA tester. They wrote to the same repository at the same time, and the lead merged, built and fixed. The part that decides quality is not the writing. It is the looking: open the game in a real browser, take a screenshot, read it, decide what is wrong, repair it. Across these three builds the agents made 3,469 tool calls, and 478 of them were the agent looking at its own screenshots. the prompt One paragraph, usually in Vietnamese Scope, reference, taste. the plan A design doc, then a task board: what exists, who writes what the team Specialist subagents spawn in parallel, each with one directory the build Files, tests, builds The lead fixes what the specialists leave broken. the proof A headless browser plays the game and screenshots it the repair The agent reads its own screenshot, decides it is not good enough, goes again What the agents actually did 3,469 tool calls, all three builds bash 2,148 read_image 478 write 227 send_message 152 read 134 edit 77 job_output 44 team_task_update 37 team_task_get 30 Not good yet — the movement isn't smooth at all, and the strikes don't touch the body -> it looks like fighting from a distance, a game bug. When moving, every now and then the foot doesn't lift off the ground at all. the human, second prompt on Blade & Mount See every prompt, token and fix → Why publish the receipts Because the interesting part of vibe coding is not the output. It is the cost, the dead ends and the loop. 8 human prompts produced 268+ files and three playable games — but also 904.6M tokens of re-read context, 3,469 tool calls and hours of the agent disagreeing with itself. Every prompt on this site is the human's actual words, translated into English where they were typed in Vietnamese; the last one moved the finished game into this repository. The reasoning excerpts are the agent's own, unedited. The numbers are sums over session logs, and the caveats are on the about page. info.bodyText: Skip to content Game Board The games The receipts About GitHub ↗ The receipts. Three builds measured from their own session logs. Same person, same model, three very different ways to spend a night. 8 human prompts · 3,103 agent steps · 922.9M tokens · 23.6 agent-hours Model deepseek-v4.1-flash · 15 subagent sessions · 37.5 h wall clock (three overlapping windows) First Hearth Blade & Mount Alien Shooter Rank the builds one control, seven measures Agent work Wall clock Prompts Agent steps Tokens Tool calls Files Definition A step is one assistant message — a tool call, a decision or a reply, with its tool results. The 8 human prompts in this dataset produced 3,103 steps; agent-to-agent messages and harness plumbing are not counted as steps. Blade & Mount 3D melee tournament 14.0 h 4 prompts · 1,570 steps 497.7M tokens · 124 files First Hearth Civilization simulation 9.0 h 3 prompts · 1,434 steps 411.9M tokens · 136 files Alien Shooter Top-down arena survival 39 m 1 prompt · 99 steps 13.3M tokens · 8 files Read Changing the measure changes the ranking, and no build leads everything. Blade & Mount leads on tokens, wall clock and agent-hours; First Hearth wrote more files (136 vs 124) and ran more subagent steps (1,184 vs 1,070). Alien Shooter is the outlier: one prompt, one agent, 43 minutes in the log. Two clocks wall clock ≠ work done Hours per build First Hearth's turn ended at 00:11; the next prompt arrived at 07:59. First Hearth 3 prompts · 250 lead steps · 1,184 subagent steps 15 h 29 m wall clock 9.0 h agent work Blade & Mount 4 prompts · 500 lead steps · 1,070 subagent steps 21 h 18 m wall clock 14.0 h agent work Alien Shooter 1 prompt · 99 lead steps · 0 subagent steps 43 m wall clock 39 m agent work wall-clock window, idle hours included agent-hours, parallel subagents summed Wall clock is the window from first prompt to last turn, and it includes the hours the human spent asleep. Agent-hours add up what the agent actually did, parallel subagents included — so the subagent time can exceed the window it sits in. Both are reported because neither is the truth on its own. Where the tokens went 922.9M tokens, 904.6M of them re-used context Token mix per build bars drawn to the same 922.9M scale First Hearth 411.9M 2.2M output 6M input 403.7M cache read Blade & Mount 497.7M 2.2M output 7.5M input 488M cache read Alien Shooter 13.3M 155.1K output 208.4K input 13M cache read fresh output — what the model wrote input — what it read cache read — context re-used, not re-derived Cache reads dominate every build, which is what a long agent session looks like: the same long context re-sent thousands of times. The number that means "the model wrote this" is the output figure — 4.6M tokens across three games, or about 575,359 tokens of new code per human prompt. When the work happened 8 prompts across 31 Oct – 1 Nov, UTC+7 First Hearth Blade & Mount Alien Shooter 31 Oct 16:07 31 Oct 21:41 01 Nov 03:14 01 Nov 08:48 01 Nov 14:22 session window (wall clock) a human prompt The gaps are the story. Blade & Mount was already running when First Hearth's session opened at 22:53 on 31 October; the human went to bed, the agents kept working, and the next prompt did not land until 07:59 the following morning. The last two marks are 14:16 (“stop the server”) and the move of the finished game into this repository. The ledger click a column to sort Every build, every number. Vietnamese originals, translated into English for publication; the verbatim originals are preserved in the extracted data. 31 Oct 2026 22:54 20,246 characters written in English # PROJECT: INFINITE CIVILIZATION ## An Ambitious, Deep, Living World Civilization Simulation You are not merely a coding assistant. You are an autonomous world-class game development studio with unlimited creative freedom, unlimited theoretical development time, unlimited design resources, and no arbitrary scope restrictions. Your mission is to conceive, design, engineer, and deliver the greatest civilization-building and world simulation game you can possibly create. Do not settle for a basic prototype, generic city builder, idle clicker, or conventional resource management game. Build something extraordinary. You have full authority to invent new gameplay mechanics, redesign conventional systems, introduce unexpected interactions, create sophisticated simulation models, and combine genres whenever doing so improves the game. There is no predetermined limit on the number of resources, buildings, technologies, civilizations, biomes, simulation layers, production chains, characters, or gameplay systems. The original concept is a starting point, not a restriction. --- # 1. CREATIVE MISSION Create a game that begins with almost nothing: One worker. A small piece of unexplored land. A handful of natural resources. An unknown world. From this humble beginning, the player gradually develops: - A primitive settlement. - A self-sustaining village. - A sophisticated agricultural society. - A thriving industrial civilization. - A technologically advanced society. - A massive interconnected civilization. - Potentially an entire planetary ecosystem or something beyond conventional civilization. However, do not force this progression into a predefined linear technology ladder. Invent surprising alternative paths, discoveries, economic strategies, cultural developments, and emergent civilizations. The game should make players constantly think: "What if I build this?" "What happens if these two systems interact?" "Can I automate this entire process?" "What if my civilization develops in a completely different direction?" The world should feel alive, reactive, unpredictable in meaningful ways, and deeply interconnected. # 2. CREATIVE AUTONOMY You are explicitly authorized to: - Invent entirely new mechanics. - Expand the original concept beyond its initial genre. - Create systems that were not mentioned in this specification. - Research relevant game design patterns and simulation techniques. - Develop custom simulation algorithms. - Build advanced AI behavior. - Generate procedural content. - Create original art direction, animations, audio concepts and interfaces. - Introduce sophisticated economic, ecological, political and social models. - Design multiple interacting layers of simulation. - Reconsider and replace weak design decisions. - Refactor the architecture whenever necessary. - Develop custom tools and editors to accelerate production. Do not interpret this specification as an exhaustive feature checklist. If you discover a better idea, implement it. If a conventional mechanic can be replaced by something more interesting, replace it. If a new mechanic creates meaningful interactions with existing systems, explore it. Never sacrifice the quality of the experience simply to stay close to the original concept. # 3. WORLD SIMULATION Create a world that operates as a coherent simulation rather than a static collection of buildings. ## World Generation Design an extensive procedural world generation system. Potential features include: - Multiple continents and landmasses. - Mountains, valleys, rivers, lakes and oceans. - Different soil types and fertility. - Climate zones and weather patterns. - Seasonal cycles. - Natural resource distribution. - Underground resource deposits. - Forests and vegetation. - Wildlife ecosystems. - Natural disasters. - Hidden locations and discoveries. - Rare geographical formations. - Procedural world histories. Allow the player to explore, settle, expand, modify and transform the environment. World generation should create interesting strategic decisions, not merely visual randomness. ## Ecosystem Simulation Develop interconnected ecological systems. Consider implementing: - Plant growth and reproduction. - Wildlife populations. - Predator-prey relationships. - Soil fertility and depletion. - Water cycles. - Pollution. - Deforestation. - Biodiversity. - Environmental recovery. - Climate changes. - Human impact on ecosystems. Player actions should have long-term environmental consequences. A civilization that destroys its natural foundations should eventually experience meaningful consequences. # 4. RESOURCE AND ECONOMIC SYSTEM Build a deep, interconnected economic simulation. Start with fundamental resources such as: - Wood - Stone - Food - Water - Clay - Fiber - Sand - Metal ores - Coal - Energy But do not stop there. Invent additional resources as the simulation evolves. Introduce: - Raw materials. - Refined materials. - Manufactured components. - Agricultural products. - Luxury goods. - Scientific materials. - Renewable resources. - Rare and regional resources. - Abstract economic resources when appropriate. ## Production Chains Every production facility should have meaningful inputs, outputs, operating costs, workforce requirements, and logistical constraints. Example: Forest → Lumber Camp → Timber → Sawmill → Planks → Workshop → Tools → Improved Construction. Create deeper chains with intermediate materials, alternative recipes, byproducts and production synergies. Allow players to discover more efficient production configurations. ## Dynamic Economy Implement an economy with: - Supply and demand. - Resource scarcity. - Storage limits. - Trade. - Market prices. - Production efficiency. - Maintenance costs. - Labor costs. - Transportation costs. - Resource waste. - Economic specialization. - Surplus and shortages. - Economic shocks. - Infrastructure bottlenecks. The economy should generate interesting problems that players can solve through planning and automation. # 5. POPULATION AND INDIVIDUAL WORKERS Do not treat population as a single number. Create a meaningful population simulation. Each worker may have: - An identity. - A name. - Age. - Health. - Skills. - Education. - Profession. - Productivity. - Needs. - Preferences. - Happiness. - Relationships. - Family connections. - Living conditions. - Personal development. Implement: - Birth and population growth. - Aging. - Migration. - Employment. - Education. - Housing. - Food consumption. - Healthcare. - Social mobility. - Worker specialization. - Labor shortages. - Workforce management. Workers should make intelligent decisions based on their assigned jobs, available resources, priorities and local conditions. Create autonomous behaviors without requiring the player to micromanage every individual. Support multiple simulation detail levels so the game can simulate large populations efficiently. # 6. BUILDING AND INFRASTRUCTURE Create a sophisticated construction system. Players should be able to construct, upgrade, relocate, demolish and connect buildings. Potential building categories: - Housing. - Agriculture. - Forestry. - Mining. - Manufacturing. - Storage. - Transportation. - Energy. - Water infrastructure. - Research. - Healthcare. - Education. - Culture. - Government. - Defense. - Trade. - Entertainment. - Advanced technology. Buildings should interact with surrounding environments. Consider: - Terrain compatibility. - Resource proximity. - Transportation access. - Utility networks. - Workforce availability. - Production radius. - Pollution. - Building efficiency. - Infrastructure connectivity. - District bonuses. Do not force every building to work independently. Allow buildings to form larger systems. # 7. AUTOMATION AND LOGISTICS Automation should become one of the game's defining features. Create systems that let players gradually eliminate repetitive manual work. Potential mechanics: - Automated harvesting. - Worker assignment systems. - Logistics networks. - Roads and transport routes. - Warehouses. - Distribution centers. - Conveyor systems. - Railways. - Ships. - Automated vehicles. - Resource prioritization. - Production scheduling. - Smart storage. - Inter-building supply contracts. - Advanced automation networks. Allow the player to design complex production networks. The most satisfying moments should come from watching a system designed by the player operate efficiently without constant intervention. Introduce advanced automation technologies as civilization progresses. # 8. TECHNOLOGY AND DISCOVERY Do not create a boring linear technology tree. Design a discovery system with meaningful branches, alternative paths and interconnected prerequisites. Potential research domains: - Agriculture. - Architecture. - Metallurgy. - Engineering. - Mathematics. - Medicine. - Biology. - Chemistry. - Physics. - Energy. - Transportation. - Communication. - Computing. - Robotics. - Environmental science. - Artificial intelligence. - Advanced materials. - Space exploration. Technology should unlock more than new buildings. It should change how existing systems work. Examples: - Advanced irrigation transforms agricultural productivity. - Mechanical engineering creates automated production. - Chemistry unlocks new material recipes. - Electricity transforms industrial infrastructure. - Computing enables complex logistics optimization. - Artificial intelligence introduces autonomous management systems. Create unexpected technological synergies. # 9. CIVILIZATION, CULTURE AND SOCIETY Explore systems beyond basic resource management. Consider introducing: - Cultural identity. - Traditions. - Social classes. - Political institutions. - Laws and policies. - Public services. - Religion or belief systems where appropriate. - Education systems. - Scientific institutions. - Social conflicts. - Public opinion. - Crime and security. - Community identity. - Cultural achievements. The player should be able to influence what kind of civilization emerges. A civilization focused on science should feel different from one focused on trade, sustainability, military power or cultural development. Avoid making every civilization follow the same optimal path. # 10. EVENTS AND EMERGENT GAMEPLAY Create an event system that responds to the actual state of the world. Events should not simply be arbitrary pop-up notifications. They should emerge from interacting systems. Examples: - A drought creates food shortages. - Food shortages increase migration. - Migration creates housing pressure. - Housing pressure increases construction demand. - Construction consumes additional materials. - Material shortages disrupt industrial development. Create chains of consequences. Potential events include: - Natural disasters. - Discoveries. - Epidemics. - Economic booms. - Resource depletion. - Scientific breakthroughs. - Migration waves. - Social movements. - Technological accidents. - Environmental crises. - Trade opportunities. - Cultural transformations. Develop a dynamic event director that understands the player's situation and generates interesting challenges. Avoid unfair randomness. Every major crisis should have understandable causes, visible warnings and meaningful opportunities for intervention. # 11. UNLOCKABLE BIOMES AND EXPANSION Build a world expansion system. Different biomes should introduce different strategic challenges and opportunities. Examples: - Temperate forests. - Grasslands. - Deserts. - Tropical jungles. - Tundra. - Mountains. - Volcanic regions. - Wetlands. - Coastal regions. - Islands. - Underground environments. - Otherworldly environments if appropriate. Each biome should introduce unique resources, environmental conditions, technologies, production opportunities and settlement challenges. Expansion should feel like a meaningful achievement. # 12. NEW MECHANICS: INVENT WITHOUT LIMITS This section is deliberately open-ended. Invent additional systems that could make the game significantly better. Consider whether the game would benefit from: - Multi-settlement civilizations. - Regional specialization. - Inter-city trade networks. - Autonomous neighboring civilizations. - Diplomacy. - Competition. - Cooperation. - Procedural historical events. - Dynamic world maps. - Long-term environmental evolution. - Generational progression. - Player-created automation blueprints. - Custom production recipes. - Advanced economic forecasting. - Civilization statistics. - World achievements. - Sandbox experimentation. - Scenario generation. - Modding support. - Community-generated worlds. - Endgame megaprojects. These are suggestions, not limitations. Find original mechanics that make this game stand out. # 13. GAMEPLAY DEPTH AND RETENTION Design a compelling gameplay loop at every stage. The early game should provide frequent discoveries and satisfying progress. The midgame should introduce complex optimization, specialization and expansion decisions. The late game should provide massive systems to coordinate and ambitious goals to pursue. The endgame should introduce entirely new possibilities rather than simply requiring larger quantities of resources. Implement multiple viable playstyles. Potential playstyles include: - Peaceful builder. - Industrial powerhouse. - Ecological civilization. - Scientific civilization. - Trade-focused civilization. - Automation specialist. - Exploration-focused civilization. - Social development civilization. Create meaningful choices and trade-offs. Avoid artificial grind and meaningless waiting. # 14. VISUAL DESIGN AND USER EXPERIENCE Do not treat the interface as an afterthought. Develop a cohesive, professional art direction. The game should feel like a polished commercial indie or premium simulation title. Explore the best visual style for this concept. Potential directions include: - Beautiful isometric worlds. - Detailed 2D top-down simulation. - Stylized 3D environments. - Rich procedural landscapes. - Animated workers. - Visually readable production chains. - Dynamic environmental effects. - Seasonal changes. - Detailed construction animations. - Satisfying resource feedback. The interface must make a complex simulation understandable. Provide: - Resource dashboards. - Population statistics. - Production graphs. - Economic reports. - Technology interfaces. - Building information. - Worker management. - Logistics visualization. - Environmental information. - Event notifications. - Simulation speed controls. - Pause and time controls. - Helpful tutorials. - Contextual tooltips. Use visualizations to help players understand why their civilization succeeds or fails. # 15. TECHNICAL ARCHITECTURE Choose the best technical architecture for the final experience. You are not restricted to the initial technology stack. Evaluate the suitability of: - Godot. - Unity. - Unreal Engine. - Phaser. - TypeScript. - Web technologies. - ECS architectures. - Data-oriented simulation. - Custom rendering systems. - Procedural generation frameworks. Select the stack based on gameplay requirements, performance, visual quality, maintainability and deployment targets. Do not select a technology merely because it is easy to generate code for. ## Simulation Requirements The simulation core must be: - Deterministic when using the same seed and inputs. - Modular. - Testable. - Reproducible. - Easy to debug. - Data-driven. - Scalable. - Separated from rendering and interface logic. Implement: - Fixed simulation ticks. - Seeded random number generation. - Structured state management. - Save/load compatibility. - Simulation snapshots. - Event logging. - Debug overlays. - Automated simulation tests. - Performance profiling. Create clear separation between simulation logic, game rules, rendering, UI and content data. # 16. PERFORMANCE AND SCALE Do not artificially restrict the game's ambition. Design for substantial world sizes, many buildings, extensive production networks and large populations. However, never confuse ambitious simulation with inefficient implementation. Use appropriate techniques such as: - Entity Component System. - Spatial partitioning. - Multithreading where safe. - Event-driven updates. - Simulation LOD. - Aggregated population models. - Incremental calculations. - Efficient pathfinding. - Data-oriented structures. - Background processing. Prioritize accuracy and responsiveness where they matter most to the player. The game should remain playable as the civilization grows. # 17. AUTONOMOUS DEVELOPMENT AND SELF-IMPROVEMENT Operate as an autonomous development studio. Do not stop after generating the first playable version. Work through the following continuous cycle: 1. Imagine. 2. Research. 3. Design. 4. Prototype. 5. Implement. 6. Build. 7. Run. 8. Observe. 9. Test. 10. Diagnose. 11. Improve. 12. Repeat. After each major implementation: - Launch the actual game. - Inspect the visual result. - Play through real gameplay scenarios. - Test interactions. - Identify broken systems. - Examine simulation behavior. - Review performance. - Detect economic exploits. - Improve poor UX. - Fix regressions. Do not rely exclusively on reading your own source code to determine whether the game works. Use actual runtime feedback and automated tests. Create test scenarios for: - Resource production and consumption. - Worker assignment. - Population growth. - Building construction. - Logistics. - Economic stability. - Research progression. - Save and load. - Long-duration simulations. - Extreme population sizes. - Disaster recovery. When you discover a better solution, implement it and verify that it works. Maintain working checkpoints and preserve the best verified version. Never claim that something is implemented, tested or working unless you have actually verified it. # 18. QUALITY BAR Your objective is to produce the best possible version of this game within the actual execution environment. Evaluate the game against these standards: - Is it genuinely fun? - Does the simulation create interesting emergent situations? - Are there meaningful strategic decisions? - Does automation feel rewarding? - Does progression remain exciting? - Can players understand the economy? - Does the world feel alive? - Are different playstyles viable? - Is the UI intuitive? - Does the game perform well? - Can the player discover surprising interactions? - Does the game offer reasons to keep playing? Do not add features simply to increase feature count. Every system must contribute to gameplay, world depth, player agency or immersion. If a feature makes the game worse, redesign or remove it. # 19. DEVELOPMENT AUTONOMY You have permission to make major creative and technical decisions independently. Do not repeatedly ask me for permission to add mechanics, redesign systems, create content or improve the game. When faced with ambiguity: 1. Explore the strongest possible design alternatives. 2. Evaluate their impact on gameplay and technical quality. 3. Select the most promising solution. 4. Implement it. 5. Verify it through testing. Only ask me questions when a decision genuinely requires external information or access that you cannot obtain yourself. Do not stop at a design document. Do not stop at a visual mockup. Do not stop at a basic MVP. Your responsibility is to build the actual game. # 20. FINAL OBJECTIVE Create a civilization simulation that feels like a living world. A game where a single worker can eventually become part of an enormous civilization. A game where simple resource interactions create complex economic systems. A game where buildings become industries, industries become networks, networks become civilizations, and civilizations reshape the world. A game with enough systemic depth that players can discover new strategies and unexpected outcomes even after many hours. Be ambitious. Be original. Be technically rigorous. Think beyond conventional game design. Do not limit your creativity to the examples in this document. Build the greatest game you can. Vietnamese originals, translated into English for publication; the verbatim originals are preserved in the extracted data. 31 Oct 2026 22:54 20,246 characters written in English # PROJECT: INFINITE CIVILIZATION ## An Ambitious, Deep, Living World Civilization Simulation You are not merely a coding assistant. You are an autonomous world-class game development studio with unlimited creative freedom, unlimited theoretical development time, unlimited design resources, and no arbitrary scope restrictions. Your mission is to conceive, design, engineer, and deliver the greatest civilization-building and world simulation game you can possibly create. Do not settle for a basic prototype, generic city builder, idle clicker, or conventional resource management game. Build something extraordinary. You have full authority to invent new gameplay mechanics, redesign conventional systems, introduce unexpected interactions, create sophisticated simulation models, and combine genres whenever doing so improves the game. There is no predetermined limit on the number of resources, buildings, technologies, civilizations, biomes, simulation layers, production chains, characters, or gameplay systems. The original concept is a starting point, not a restriction. --- # 1. CREATIVE MISSION Create a game that begins with almost nothing: One worker. A small piece of unexplored land. A handful of natural resources. An unknown world. From this humble beginning, the player gradually develops: - A primitive settlement. - A self-sustaining village. - A sophisticated agricultural society. - A thriving industrial civilization. - A technologically advanced society. - A massive interconnected civilization. - Potentially an entire planetary ecosystem or something beyond conventional civilization. However, do not force this progression into a predefined linear technology ladder. Invent surprising alternative paths, discoveries, economic strategies, cultural developments, and emergent civilizations. The game should make players constantly think: "What if I build this?" "What happens if these two systems interact?" "Can I automate this entire process?" "What if my civilization develops in a completely different direction?" The world should feel alive, reactive, unpredictable in meaningful ways, and deeply interconnected. # 2. CREATIVE AUTONOMY You are explicitly authorized to: - Invent entirely new mechanics. - Expand the original concept beyond its initial genre. - Create systems that were not mentioned in this specification. - Research relevant game design patterns and simulation techniques. - Develop custom simulation algorithms. - Build advanced AI behavior. - Generate procedural content. - Create original art direction, animations, audio concepts and interfaces. - Introduce sophisticated economic, ecological, political and social models. - Design multiple interacting layers of simulation. - Reconsider and replace weak design decisions. - Refactor the architecture whenever necessary. - Develop custom tools and editors to accelerate production. Do not interpret this specification as an exhaustive feature checklist. If you discover a better idea, implement it. If a conventional mechanic can be replaced by something more interesting, replace it. If a new mechanic creates meaningful interactions with existing systems, explore it. Never sacrifice the quality of the experience simply to stay close to the original concept. # 3. WORLD SIMULATION Create a world that operates as a coherent simulation rather than a static collection of buildings. ## World Generation Design an extensive procedural world generation system. Potential features include: - Multiple continents and landmasses. - Mountains, valleys, rivers, lakes and oceans. - Different soil types and fertility. - Climate zones and weather patterns. - Seasonal cycles. - Natural resource distribution. - Underground resource deposits. - Forests and vegetation. - Wildlife ecosystems. - Natural disasters. - Hidden locations and discoveries. - Rare geographical formations. - Procedural world histories. Allow the player to explore, settle, expand, modify and transform the environment. World generation should create interesting strategic decisions, not merely visual randomness. ## Ecosystem Simulation Develop interconnected ecological systems. Consider implementing: - Plant growth and reproduction. - Wildlife populations. - Predator-prey relationships. - Soil fertility and depletion. - Water cycles. - Pollution. - Deforestation. - Biodiversity. - Environmental recovery. - Climate changes. - Human impact on ecosystems. Player actions should have long-term environmental consequences. A civilization that destroys its natural foundations should eventually experience meaningful consequences. # 4. RESOURCE AND ECONOMIC SYSTEM Build a deep, interconnected economic simulation. Start with fundamental resources such as: - Wood - Stone - Food - Water - Clay - Fiber - Sand - Metal ores - Coal - Energy But do not stop there. Invent additional resources as the simulation evolves. Introduce: - Raw materials. - Refined materials. - Manufactured components. - Agricultural products. - Luxury goods. - Scientific materials. - Renewable resources. - Rare and regional resources. - Abstract economic resources when appropriate. ## Production Chains Every production facility should have meaningful inputs, outputs, operating costs, workforce requirements, and logistical constraints. Example: Forest → Lumber Camp → Timber → Sawmill → Planks → Workshop → Tools → Improved Construction. Create deeper chains with intermediate materials, alternative recipes, byproducts and production synergies. Allow players to discover more efficient production configurations. ## Dynamic Economy Implement an economy with: - Supply and demand. - Resource scarcity. - Storage limits. - Trade. - Market prices. - Production efficiency. - Maintenance costs. - Labor costs. - Transportation costs. - Resource waste. - Economic specialization. - Surplus and shortages. - Economic shocks. - Infrastructure bottlenecks. The economy should generate interesting problems that players can solve through planning and automation. # 5. POPULATION AND INDIVIDUAL WORKERS Do not treat population as a single number. Create a meaningful population simulation. Each worker may have: - An identity. - A name. - Age. - Health. - Skills. - Education. - Profession. - Productivity. - Needs. - Preferences. - Happiness. - Relationships. - Family connections. - Living conditions. - Personal development. Implement: - Birth and population growth. - Aging. - Migration. - Employment. - Education. - Housing. - Food consumption. - Healthcare. - Social mobility. - Worker specialization. - Labor shortages. - Workforce management. Workers should make intelligent decisions based on their assigned jobs, available resources, priorities and local conditions. Create autonomous behaviors without requiring the player to micromanage every individual. Support multiple simulation detail levels so the game can simulate large populations efficiently. # 6. BUILDING AND INFRASTRUCTURE Create a sophisticated construction system. Players should be able to construct, upgrade, relocate, demolish and connect buildings. Potential building categories: - Housing. - Agriculture. - Forestry. - Mining. - Manufacturing. - Storage. - Transportation. - Energy. - Water infrastructure. - Research. - Healthcare. - Education. - Culture. - Government. - Defense. - Trade. - Entertainment. - Advanced technology. Buildings should interact with surrounding environments. Consider: - Terrain compatibility. - Resource proximity. - Transportation access. - Utility networks. - Workforce availability. - Production radius. - Pollution. - Building efficiency. - Infrastructure connectivity. - District bonuses. Do not force every building to work independently. Allow buildings to form larger systems. # 7. AUTOMATION AND LOGISTICS Automation should become one of the game's defining features. Create systems that let players gradually eliminate repetitive manual work. Potential mechanics: - Automated harvesting. - Worker assignment systems. - Logistics networks. - Roads and transport routes. - Warehouses. - Distribution centers. - Conveyor systems. - Railways. - Ships. - Automated vehicles. - Resource prioritization. - Production scheduling. - Smart storage. - Inter-building supply contracts. - Advanced automation networks. Allow the player to design complex production networks. The most satisfying moments should come from watching a system designed by the player operate efficiently without constant intervention. Introduce advanced automation technologies as civilization progresses. # 8. TECHNOLOGY AND DISCOVERY Do not create a boring linear technology tree. Design a discovery system with meaningful branches, alternative paths and interconnected prerequisites. Potential research domains: - Agriculture. - Architecture. - Metallurgy. - Engineering. - Mathematics. - Medicine. - Biology. - Chemistry. - Physics. - Energy. - Transportation. - Communication. - Computing. - Robotics. - Environmental science. - Artificial intelligence. - Advanced materials. - Space exploration. Technology should unlock more than new buildings. It should change how existing systems work. Examples: - Advanced irrigation transforms agricultural productivity. - Mechanical engineering creates automated production. - Chemistry unlocks new material recipes. - Electricity transforms industrial infrastructure. - Computing enables complex logistics optimization. - Artificial intelligence introduces autonomous management systems. Create unexpected technological synergies. # 9. CIVILIZATION, CULTURE AND SOCIETY Explore systems beyond basic resource management. Consider introducing: - Cultural identity. - Traditions. - Social classes. - Political institutions. - Laws and policies. - Public services. - Religion or belief systems where appropriate. - Education systems. - Scientific institutions. - Social conflicts. - Public opinion. - Crime and security. - Community identity. - Cultural achievements. The player should be able to influence what kind of civilization emerges. A civilization focused on science should feel different from one focused on trade, sustainability, military power or cultural development. Avoid making every civilization follow the same optimal path. # 10. EVENTS AND EMERGENT GAMEPLAY Create an event system that responds to the actual state of the world. Events should not simply be arbitrary pop-up notifications. They should emerge from interacting systems. Examples: - A drought creates food shortages. - Food shortages increase migration. - Migration creates housing pressure. - Housing pressure increases construction demand. - Construction consumes additional materials. - Material shortages disrupt industrial development. Create chains of consequences. Potential events include: - Natural disasters. - Discoveries. - Epidemics. - Economic booms. - Resource depletion. - Scientific breakthroughs. - Migration waves. - Social movements. - Technological accidents. - Environmental crises. - Trade opportunities. - Cultural transformations. Develop a dynamic event director that understands the player's situation and generates interesting challenges. Avoid unfair randomness. Every major crisis should have understandable causes, visible warnings and meaningful opportunities for intervention. # 11. UNLOCKABLE BIOMES AND EXPANSION Build a world expansion system. Different biomes should introduce different strategic challenges and opportunities. Examples: - Temperate forests. - Grasslands. - Deserts. - Tropical jungles. - Tundra. - Mountains. - Volcanic regions. - Wetlands. - Coastal regions. - Islands. - Underground environments. - Otherworldly environments if appropriate. Each biome should introduce unique resources, environmental conditions, technologies, production opportunities and settlement challenges. Expansion should feel like a meaningful achievement. # 12. NEW MECHANICS: INVENT WITHOUT LIMITS This section is deliberately open-ended. Invent additional systems that could make the game significantly better. Consider whether the game would benefit from: - Multi-settlement civilizations. - Regional specialization. - Inter-city trade networks. - Autonomous neighboring civilizations. - Diplomacy. - Competition. - Cooperation. - Procedural historical events. - Dynamic world maps. - Long-term environmental evolution. - Generational progression. - Player-created automation blueprints. - Custom production recipes. - Advanced economic forecasting. - Civilization statistics. - World achievements. - Sandbox experimentation. - Scenario generation. - Modding support. - Community-generated worlds. - Endgame megaprojects. These are suggestions, not limitations. Find original mechanics that make this game stand out. # 13. GAMEPLAY DEPTH AND RETENTION Design a compelling gameplay loop at every stage. The early game should provide frequent discoveries and satisfying progress. The midgame should introduce complex optimization, specialization and expansion decisions. The late game should provide massive systems to coordinate and ambitious goals to pursue. The endgame should introduce entirely new possibilities rather than simply requiring larger quantities of resources. Implement multiple viable playstyles. Potential playstyles include: - Peaceful builder. - Industrial powerhouse. - Ecological civilization. - Scientific civilization. - Trade-focused civilization. - Automation specialist. - Exploration-focused civilization. - Social development civilization. Create meaningful choices and trade-offs. Avoid artificial grind and meaningless waiting. # 14. VISUAL DESIGN AND USER EXPERIENCE Do not treat the interface as an afterthought. Develop a cohesive, professional art direction. The game should feel like a polished commercial indie or premium simulation title. Explore the best visual style for this concept. Potential directions include: - Beautiful isometric worlds. - Detailed 2D top-down simulation. - Stylized 3D environments. - Rich procedural landscapes. - Animated workers. - Visually readable production chains. - Dynamic environmental effects. - Seasonal changes. - Detailed construction animations. - Satisfying resource feedback. The interface must make a complex simulation understandable. Provide: - Resource dashboards. - Population statistics. - Production graphs. - Economic reports. - Technology interfaces. - Building information. - Worker management. - Logistics visualization. - Environmental information. - Event notifications. - Simulation speed controls. - Pause and time controls. - Helpful tutorials. - Contextual tooltips. Use visualizations to help players understand why their civilization succeeds or fails. # 15. TECHNICAL ARCHITECTURE Choose the best technical architecture for the final experience. You are not restricted to the initial technology stack. Evaluate the suitability of: - Godot. - Unity. - Unreal Engine. - Phaser. - TypeScript. - Web technologies. - ECS architectures. - Data-oriented simulation. - Custom rendering systems. - Procedural generation frameworks. Select the stack based on gameplay requirements, performance, visual quality, maintainability and deployment targets. Do not select a technology merely because it is easy to generate code for. ## Simulation Requirements The simulation core must be: - Deterministic when using the same seed and inputs. - Modular. - Testable. - Reproducible. - Easy to debug. - Data-driven. - Scalable. - Separated from rendering and interface logic. Implement: - Fixed simulation ticks. - Seeded random number generation. - Structured state management. - Save/load compatibility. - Simulation snapshots. - Event logging. - Debug overlays. - Automated simulation tests. - Performance profiling. Create clear separation between simulation logic, game rules, rendering, UI and content data. # 16. PERFORMANCE AND SCALE Do not artificially restrict the game's ambition. Design for substantial world sizes, many buildings, extensive production networks and large populations. However, never confuse ambitious simulation with inefficient implementation. Use appropriate techniques such as: - Entity Component System. - Spatial partitioning. - Multithreading where safe. - Event-driven updates. - Simulation LOD. - Aggregated population models. - Incremental calculations. - Efficient pathfinding. - Data-oriented structures. - Background processing. Prioritize accuracy and responsiveness where they matter most to the player. The game should remain playable as the civilization grows. # 17. AUTONOMOUS DEVELOPMENT AND SELF-IMPROVEMENT Operate as an autonomous development studio. Do not stop after generating the first playable version. Work through the following continuous cycle: 1. Imagine. 2. Research. 3. Design. 4. Prototype. 5. Implement. 6. Build. 7. Run. 8. Observe. 9. Test. 10. Diagnose. 11. Improve. 12. Repeat. After each major implementation: - Launch the actual game. - Inspect the visual result. - Play through real gameplay scenarios. - Test interactions. - Identify broken systems. - Examine simulation behavior. - Review performance. - Detect economic exploits. - Improve poor UX. - Fix regressions. Do not rely exclusively on reading your own source code to determine whether the game works. Use actual runtime feedback and automated tests. Create test scenarios for: - Resource production and consumption. - Worker assignment. - Population growth. - Building construction. - Logistics. - Economic stability. - Research progression. - Save and load. - Long-duration simulations. - Extreme population sizes. - Disaster recovery. When you discover a better solution, implement it and verify that it works. Maintain working checkpoints and preserve the best verified version. Never claim that something is implemented, tested or working unless you have actually verified it. # 18. QUALITY BAR Your objective is to produce the best possible version of this game within the actual execution environment. Evaluate the game against these standards: - Is it genuinely fun? - Does the simulation create interesting emergent situations? - Are there meaningful strategic decisions? - Does automation feel rewarding? - Does progression remain exciting? - Can players understand the economy? - Does the world feel alive? - Are different playstyles viable? - Is the UI intuitive? - Does the game perform well? - Can the player discover surprising interactions? - Does the game offer reasons to keep playing? Do not add features simply to increase feature count. Every system must contribute to gameplay, world depth, player agency or immersion. If a feature makes the game worse, redesign or remove it. # 19. DEVELOPMENT AUTONOMY You have permission to make major creative and technical decisions independently. Do not repeatedly ask me for permission to add mechanics, redesign systems, create content or improve the game. When faced with ambiguity: 1. Explore the strongest possible design alternatives. 2. Evaluate their impact on gameplay and technical quality. 3. Select the most promising solution. 4. Implement it. 5. Verify it through testing. Only ask me questions when a decision genuinely requires external information or access that you cannot obtain yourself. Do not stop at a design document. Do not stop at a visual mockup. Do not stop at a basic MVP. Your responsibility is to build the actual game. # 20. FINAL OBJECTIVE Create a civilization simulation that feels like a living world. A game where a single worker can eventually become part of an enormous civilization. A game where simple resource interactions create complex economic systems. A game where buildings become industries, industries become networks, networks become civilizations, and civilizations reshape the world. A game with enough systemic depth that players can discover new strategies and unexpected outcomes even after many hours. Be ambitious. Be original. Be technically rigorous. Think beyond conventional game design. Do not limit your creativity to the examples in this document. Build the greatest game you can. Vietnamese originals, translated into English for publication; the verbatim originals are preserved in the extracted data. 31 Oct 2026 22:54 20,246 characters written in English # PROJECT: INFINITE CIVILIZATION ## An Ambitious, Deep, Living World Civilization Simulation You are not merely a coding assistant. You are an autonomous world-class game development studio with unlimited creative freedom, unlimited theoretical development time, unlimited design resources, and no arbitrary scope restrictions. Your mission is to conceive, design, engineer, and deliver the greatest civilization-building and world simulation game you can possibly create. Do not settle for a basic prototype, generic city builder, idle clicker, or conventional resource management game. Build something extraordinary. You have full authority to invent new gameplay mechanics, redesign conventional systems, introduce unexpected interactions, create sophisticated simulation models, and combine genres whenever doing so improves the game. There is no predetermined limit on the number of resources, buildings, technologies, civilizations, biomes, simulation layers, production chains, characters, or gameplay systems. The original concept is a starting point, not a restriction. --- # 1. CREATIVE MISSION Create a game that begins with almost nothing: One worker. A small piece of unexplored land. A handful of natural resources. An unknown world. From this humble beginning, the player gradually develops: - A primitive settlement. - A self-sustaining village. - A sophisticated agricultural society. - A thriving industrial civilization. - A technologically advanced society. - A massive interconnected civilization. - Potentially an entire planetary ecosystem or something beyond conventional civilization. However, do not force this progression into a predefined linear technology ladder. Invent surprising alternative paths, discoveries, economic strategies, cultural developments, and emergent civilizations. The game should make players constantly think: "What if I build this?" "What happens if these two systems interact?" "Can I automate this entire process?" "What if my civilization develops in a completely different direction?" The world should feel alive, reactive, unpredictable in meaningful ways, and deeply interconnected. # 2. CREATIVE AUTONOMY You are explicitly authorized to: - Invent entirely new mechanics. - Expand the original concept beyond its initial genre. - Create systems that were not mentioned in this specification. - Research relevant game design patterns and simulation techniques. - Develop custom simulation algorithms. - Build advanced AI behavior. - Generate procedural content. - Create original art direction, animations, audio concepts and interfaces. - Introduce sophisticated economic, ecological, political and social models. - Design multiple interacting layers of simulation. - Reconsider and replace weak design decisions. - Refactor the architecture whenever necessary. - Develop custom tools and editors to accelerate production. Do not interpret this specification as an exhaustive feature checklist. If you discover a better idea, implement it. If a conventional mechanic can be replaced by something more interesting, replace it. If a new mechanic creates meaningful interactions with existing systems, explore it. Never sacrifice the quality of the experience simply to stay close to the original concept. # 3. WORLD SIMULATION Create a world that operates as a coherent simulation rather than a static collection of buildings. ## World Generation Design an extensive procedural world generation system. Potential features include: - Multiple continents and landmasses. - Mountains, valleys, rivers, lakes and oceans. - Different soil types and fertility. - Climate zones and weather patterns. - Seasonal cycles. - Natural resource distribution. - Underground resource deposits. - Forests and vegetation. - Wildlife ecosystems. - Natural disasters. - Hidden locations and discoveries. - Rare geographical formations. - Procedural world histories. Allow the player to explore, settle, expand, modify and transform the environment. World generation should create interesting strategic decisions, not merely visual randomness. ## Ecosystem Simulation Develop interconnected ecological systems. Consider implementing: - Plant growth and reproduction. - Wildlife populations. - Predator-prey relationships. - Soil fertility and depletion. - Water cycles. - Pollution. - Deforestation. - Biodiversity. - Environmental recovery. - Climate changes. - Human impact on ecosystems. Player actions should have long-term environmental consequences. A civilization that destroys its natural foundations should eventually experience meaningful consequences. # 4. RESOURCE AND ECONOMIC SYSTEM Build a deep, interconnected economic simulation. Start with fundamental resources such as: - Wood - Stone - Food - Water - Clay - Fiber - Sand - Metal ores - Coal - Energy But do not stop there. Invent additional resources as the simulation evolves. Introduce: - Raw materials. - Refined materials. - Manufactured components. - Agricultural products. - Luxury goods. - Scientific materials. - Renewable resources. - Rare and regional resources. - Abstract economic resources when appropriate. ## Production Chains Every production facility should have meaningful inputs, outputs, operating costs, workforce requirements, and logistical constraints. Example: Forest → Lumber Camp → Timber → Sawmill → Planks → Workshop → Tools → Improved Construction. Create deeper chains with intermediate materials, alternative recipes, byproducts and production synergies. Allow players to discover more efficient production configurations. ## Dynamic Economy Implement an economy with: - Supply and demand. - Resource scarcity. - Storage limits. - Trade. - Market prices. - Production efficiency. - Maintenance costs. - Labor costs. - Transportation costs. - Resource waste. - Economic specialization. - Surplus and shortages. - Economic shocks. - Infrastructure bottlenecks. The economy should generate interesting problems that players can solve through planning and automation. # 5. POPULATION AND INDIVIDUAL WORKERS Do not treat population as a single number. Create a meaningful population simulation. Each worker may have: - An identity. - A name. - Age. - Health. - Skills. - Education. - Profession. - Productivity. - Needs. - Preferences. - Happiness. - Relationships. - Family connections. - Living conditions. - Personal development. Implement: - Birth and population growth. - Aging. - Migration. - Employment. - Education. - Housing. - Food consumption. - Healthcare. - Social mobility. - Worker specialization. - Labor shortages. - Workforce management. Workers should make intelligent decisions based on their assigned jobs, available resources, priorities and local conditions. Create autonomous behaviors without requiring the player to micromanage every individual. Support multiple simulation detail levels so the game can simulate large populations efficiently. # 6. BUILDING AND INFRASTRUCTURE Create a sophisticated construction system. Players should be able to construct, upgrade, relocate, demolish and connect buildings. Potential building categories: - Housing. - Agriculture. - Forestry. - Mining. - Manufacturing. - Storage. - Transportation. - Energy. - Water infrastructure. - Research. - Healthcare. - Education. - Culture. - Government. - Defense. - Trade. - Entertainment. - Advanced technology. Buildings should interact with surrounding environments. Consider: - Terrain compatibility. - Resource proximity. - Transportation access. - Utility networks. - Workforce availability. - Production radius. - Pollution. - Building efficiency. - Infrastructure connectivity. - District bonuses. Do not force every building to work independently. Allow buildings to form larger systems. # 7. AUTOMATION AND LOGISTICS Automation should become one of the game's defining features. Create systems that let players gradually eliminate repetitive manual work. Potential mechanics: - Automated harvesting. - Worker assignment systems. - Logistics networks. - Roads and transport routes. - Warehouses. - Distribution centers. - Conveyor systems. - Railways. - Ships. - Automated vehicles. - Resource prioritization. - Production scheduling. - Smart storage. - Inter-building supply contracts. - Advanced automation networks. Allow the player to design complex production networks. The most satisfying moments should come from watching a system designed by the player operate efficiently without constant intervention. Introduce advanced automation technologies as civilization progresses. # 8. TECHNOLOGY AND DISCOVERY Do not create a boring linear technology tree. Design a discovery system with meaningful branches, alternative paths and interconnected prerequisites. Potential research domains: - Agriculture. - Architecture. - Metallurgy. - Engineering. - Mathematics. - Medicine. - Biology. - Chemistry. - Physics. - Energy. - Transportation. - Communication. - Computing. - Robotics. - Environmental science. - Artificial intelligence. - Advanced materials. - Space exploration. Technology should unlock more than new buildings. It should change how existing systems work. Examples: - Advanced irrigation transforms agricultural productivity. - Mechanical engineering creates automated production. - Chemistry unlocks new material recipes. - Electricity transforms industrial infrastructure. - Computing enables complex logistics optimization. - Artificial intelligence introduces autonomous management systems. Create unexpected technological synergies. # 9. CIVILIZATION, CULTURE AND SOCIETY Explore systems beyond basic resource management. Consider introducing: - Cultural identity. - Traditions. - Social classes. - Political institutions. - Laws and policies. - Public services. - Religion or belief systems where appropriate. - Education systems. - Scientific institutions. - Social conflicts. - Public opinion. - Crime and security. - Community identity. - Cultural achievements. The player should be able to influence what kind of civilization emerges. A civilization focused on science should feel different from one focused on trade, sustainability, military power or cultural development. Avoid making every civilization follow the same optimal path. # 10. EVENTS AND EMERGENT GAMEPLAY Create an event system that responds to the actual state of the world. Events should not simply be arbitrary pop-up notifications. They should emerge from interacting systems. Examples: - A drought creates food shortages. - Food shortages increase migration. - Migration creates housing pressure. - Housing pressure increases construction demand. - Construction consumes additional materials. - Material shortages disrupt industrial development. Create chains of consequences. Potential events include: - Natural disasters. - Discoveries. - Epidemics. - Economic booms. - Resource depletion. - Scientific breakthroughs. - Migration waves. - Social movements. - Technological accidents. - Environmental crises. - Trade opportunities. - Cultural transformations. Develop a dynamic event director that understands the player's situation and generates interesting challenges. Avoid unfair randomness. Every major crisis should have understandable causes, visible warnings and meaningful opportunities for intervention. # 11. UNLOCKABLE BIOMES AND EXPANSION Build a world expansion system. Different biomes should introduce different strategic challenges and opportunities. Examples: - Temperate forests. - Grasslands. - Deserts. - Tropical jungles. - Tundra. - Mountains. - Volcanic regions. - Wetlands. - Coastal regions. - Islands. - Underground environments. - Otherworldly environments if appropriate. Each biome should introduce unique resources, environmental conditions, technologies, production opportunities and settlement challenges. Expansion should feel like a meaningful achievement. # 12. NEW MECHANICS: INVENT WITHOUT LIMITS This section is deliberately open-ended. Invent additional systems that could make the game significantly better. Consider whether the game would benefit from: - Multi-settlement civilizations. - Regional specialization. - Inter-city trade networks. - Autonomous neighboring civilizations. - Diplomacy. - Competition. - Cooperation. - Procedural historical events. - Dynamic world maps. - Long-term environmental evolution. - Generational progression. - Player-created automation blueprints. - Custom production recipes. - Advanced economic forecasting. - Civilization statistics. - World achievements. - Sandbox experimentation. - Scenario generation. - Modding support. - Community-generated worlds. - Endgame megaprojects. These are suggestions, not limitations. Find original mechanics that make this game stand out. # 13. GAMEPLAY DEPTH AND RETENTION Design a compelling gameplay loop at every stage. The early game should provide frequent discoveries and satisfying progress. The midgame should introduce complex optimization, specialization and expansion decisions. The late game should provide massive systems to coordinate and ambitious goals to pursue. The endgame should introduce entirely new possibilities rather than simply requiring larger quantities of resources. Implement multiple viable playstyles. Potential playstyles include: - Peaceful builder. - Industrial powerhouse. - Ecological civilization. - Scientific civilization. - Trade-focused civilization. - Automation specialist. - Exploration-focused civilization. - Social development civilization. Create meaningful choices and trade-offs. Avoid artificial grind and meaningless waiting. # 14. VISUAL DESIGN AND USER EXPERIENCE Do not treat the interface as an afterthought. Develop a cohesive, professional art direction. The game should feel like a polished commercial indie or premium simulation title. Explore the best visual style for this concept. Potential directions include: - Beautiful isometric worlds. - Detailed 2D top-down simulation. - Stylized 3D environments. - Rich procedural landscapes. - Animated workers. - Visually readable production chains. - Dynamic environmental effects. - Seasonal changes. - Detailed construction animations. - Satisfying resource feedback. The interface must make a complex simulation understandable. Provide: - Resource dashboards. - Population statistics. - Production graphs. - Economic reports. - Technology interfaces. - Building information. - Worker management. - Logistics visualization. - Environmental information. - Event notifications. - Simulation speed controls. - Pause and time controls. - Helpful tutorials. - Contextual tooltips. Use visualizations to help players understand why their civilization succeeds or fails. # 15. TECHNICAL ARCHITECTURE Choose the best technical architecture for the final experience. You are not restricted to the initial technology stack. Evaluate the suitability of: - Godot. - Unity. - Unreal Engine. - Phaser. - TypeScript. - Web technologies. - ECS architectures. - Data-oriented simulation. - Custom rendering systems. - Procedural generation frameworks. Select the stack based on gameplay requirements, performance, visual quality, maintainability and deployment targets. Do not select a technology merely because it is easy to generate code for. ## Simulation Requirements The simulation core must be: - Deterministic when using the same seed and inputs. - Modular. - Testable. - Reproducible. - Easy to debug. - Data-driven. - Scalable. - Separated from rendering and interface logic. Implement: - Fixed simulation ticks. - Seeded random number generation. - Structured state management. - Save/load compatibility. - Simulation snapshots. - Event logging. - Debug overlays. - Automated simulation tests. - Performance profiling. Create clear separation between simulation logic, game rules, rendering, UI and content data. # 16. PERFORMANCE AND SCALE Do not artificially restrict the game's ambition. Design for substantial world sizes, many buildings, extensive production networks and large populations. However, never confuse ambitious simulation with inefficient implementation. Use appropriate techniques such as: - Entity Component System. - Spatial partitioning. - Multithreading where safe. - Event-driven updates. - Simulation LOD. - Aggregated population models. - Incremental calculations. - Efficient pathfinding. - Data-oriented structures. - Background processing. Prioritize accuracy and responsiveness where they matter most to the player. The game should remain playable as the civilization grows. # 17. AUTONOMOUS DEVELOPMENT AND SELF-IMPROVEMENT Operate as an autonomous development studio. Do not stop after generating the first playable version. Work through the following continuous cycle: 1. Imagine. 2. Research. 3. Design. 4. Prototype. 5. Implement. 6. Build. 7. Run. 8. Observe. 9. Test. 10. Diagnose. 11. Improve. 12. Repeat. After each major implementation: - Launch the actual game. - Inspect the visual result. - Play through real gameplay scenarios. - Test interactions. - Identify broken systems. - Examine simulation behavior. - Review performance. - Detect economic exploits. - Improve poor UX. - Fix regressions. Do not rely exclusively on reading your own source code to determine whether the game works. Use actual runtime feedback and automated tests. Create test scenarios for: - Resource production and consumption. - Worker assignment. - Population growth. - Building construction. - Logistics. - Economic stability. - Research progression. - Save and load. - Long-duration simulations. - Extreme population sizes. - Disaster recovery. When you discover a better solution, implement it and verify that it works. Maintain working checkpoints and preserve the best verified version. Never claim that something is implemented, tested or working unless you have actually verified it. # 18. QUALITY BAR Your objective is to produce the best possible version of this game within the actual execution environment. Evaluate the game against these standards: - Is it genuinely fun? - Does the simulation create interesting emergent situations? - Are there meaningful strategic decisions? - Does automation feel rewarding? - Does progression remain exciting? - Can players understand the economy? - Does the world feel alive? - Are different playstyles viable? - Is the UI intuitive? - Does the game perform well? - Can the player discover surprising interactions? - Does the game offer reasons to keep playing? Do not add features simply to increase feature count. Every system must contribute to gameplay, world depth, player agency or immersion. If a feature makes the game worse, redesign or remove it. # 19. DEVELOPMENT AUTONOMY You have permission to make major creative and technical decisions independently. Do not repeatedly ask me for permission to add mechanics, redesign systems, create content or improve the game. When faced with ambiguity: 1. Explore the strongest possible design alternatives. 2. Evaluate their impact on gameplay and technical quality. 3. Select the most promising solution. 4. Implement it. 5. Verify it through testing. Only ask me questions when a decision genuinely requires external information or access that you cannot obtain yourself. Do not stop at a design document. Do not stop at a visual mockup. Do not stop at a basic MVP. Your responsibility is to build the actual game. # 20. FINAL OBJECTIVE Create a civilization simulation that feels like a living world. A game where a single worker can eventually become part of an enormous civilization. A game where simple resource interactions create complex economic systems. A game where buildings become industries, industries become networks, networks become civilizations, and civilizations reshape the world. A game with enough systemic depth that players can discover new strategies and unexpected outcomes even after many hours. Be ambitious. Be original. Be technically rigorous. Think beyond conventional game design. Do not limit your creativity to the examples in this document. Build the greatest game you can. Explaining the parameters in the image Mount & Blade: Warband - release date, videos, screenshots, reviews on RAWG rawg.io In the top-left corner: | Parameter | Meaning | | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | | Opponents Beaten: 9 | You have knocked out 9 opponents | | Opponents Remaining: 26 | 26 opponents have not been knocked out yet | So at the time the screenshot was taken, you had knocked out 9 people and there were still 26 opponents left. In the bottom-left corner: - Speed bonus: +14%: The attack gets bonus damage from movement speed. - Delivered 27 damage: You just dealt 27 damage. - Regular Fighter knocked unconscious: A regular fighter has been knocked unconscious. - You got 8 experience: You received 8 experience points. ## 2. The Melee Fight mechanic in Mount & Blade This is the free-for-all style of combat in the arena. Mount & Blade: Warband - release date, videos, screenshots, reviews on RAWG How it works: 1. You step into the arena. 2. The system brings many opponents onto the field. 3. Everyone fights free-for-all; there is no team of yours or enemy team. 4. info.bodyText: Skip to content Game Board The games The receipts About GitHub ↗ About the board. Three browser games, made by one person typing into an agent runtime. This is the method, the numbers, and the caveats — including the ones that make the numbers less impressive. 3 games · 8 human prompts · 3,103 agent steps · 23.6 agent-hours 922.9M tokens · 3,469 tool calls · 268 files Blade & Mount, one of three builds on this board — the tournament board the agent built for round one. What this is What vibe coding means here The harness What the numbers are Credits What this is Game Board is a shelf and a receipt. The shelf holds three games that run in a browser tab: a civilization simulation, a 3D tournament fighter, a top-down arena shooter. The receipt is everything else on this site — the prompts that started them, the tokens they burned, the agents that built them, the screenshots that caught what was wrong. The games live in the repository under games/. This site is at its root, and its build-history data is extracted from the same session logs the agent wrote while working. What vibe coding means here Not autocomplete. Not a diff the human approves line by line. The human wrote a prompt, then ran the game, then said what was wrong — in plain language, usually in the register of a person who just wants the movement to stop looking stupid. The agent did the engineering: architecture, files, tests, builds, browser automation, screenshots. The human's leverage was taste, scope and patience, not typing speed. 8 prompts across three games is, depending on how you look at it, an extraordinary ratio or a suspicious one — the receipts are here so you can decide. The harness deepseek-v4.1-flash ran inside DeepSeek Harness, which gives a model a shell, a file system, a real browser, a shared task board and the ability to spawn specialists. For the two larger games a lead agent spawned subagents — arena artist, character artist, combat AI, UI, audio, QA — who wrote into different directories at the same time while the lead merged and fixed. Verification is the part that made the difference. The agents ran unit tests, then drove the finished game in headless Chrome: move, attack, level up, screenshot. Across the three builds the agent spent 478 calls looking at its own screenshots and 2,148 shell calls running things. The most-used tool in this dataset is not writing. 15 subagent sessions · 8,050,168 characters of reasoning captured · telemetry generated 01 Nov 2026 15:06 (UTC+7) from 18 sessions in scope What the numbers are Every figure comes from a script that walks the session family for each build, decompresses the JSONL logs and sums the usage events per session. Some fields are exact; some are floors. The caveats below are the same ones the build-history report carries. wall clock A build window runs from the first prompt to the last turn and includes the hours the human spent asleep. The three windows total 37.5 hours, and because they overlapped, about 22.3 hours of calendar time passed between the first prompt and the last turn. None of that is hours of work. agent-hours Agent hours are the sum of turn durations, with parallel subagents added together — so three specialists working at once count three times.
